header:
The Ingenious Green Shoot
The heavy element M was first discovered by the British chemist William Crookes (1832-1919) while he was analyzing selenium-containing flue dust sent from a German sulfuric-acid factory. On observing through a spectroscope a bright emerald-green spectral line never seen before, he concluded that he had discovered a new element. Elemental M is silvery white and extremely soft, leaves a dark-gray streak on paper, and rapidly tarnishes when a freshly cut surface is exposed to air. M has two common oxidation states: the lower oxidation state is stable in aqueous solution, whereas compounds in the higher oxidation state readily decompose on heating and are strong oxidants.
When heated in air to approximately 300 °C, M burns to form black hygroscopic solid A. A dissolves in water to give a clear colorless solution containing the strong base B, whose aqueous basicity is close to that of KOH. Passing excess $CO_2$ through a solution of B precipitates colorless crystals C. Mixing C with nitric acid and potassium chromate solution gives yellow precipitate D (reaction 1). Adding hydrogen peroxide to a solution of B produces dark-brown powder E (reaction 2). Heating E with a KI solution acidified with hydrochloric acid gives yellow precipitate F and purple-black solid G (reaction 3). The mass fraction of M in F is 61.69 %.

subquestions.text_open: 1.1.1 Identify element M and write the chemical formulas of A-G.

1.2 The chlorides of M have unusual properties. Its lower-valent chloride H is a white solid but gradually turns purple in sunlight. Its higher-valent chloride J can be prepared from H by the combined action of concentrated hydrochloric acid and chlorine. Dissolving J in concentrated hydrochloric acid gives the tetrahedral complex anion K.
1.2.1 Write the equation for the gradual photochemical conversion of H to the purple material, and explain the composition and origin of the color of the purple product.
1.2.4 Experimentally, H is much more stable than J. Explain the key atomic-structure effect responsible for this behavior and why it is especially pronounced for M within its group.

1.3 The following experiment is performed to determine the cumulative stability constant $\beta_4$ of complex anion K formed when J dissolves in hydrochloric acid.
Step 1: Accurately weigh a quantity of J, dissolve it in 0.500 mol·L$^{-1}$ HCl, and dilute to 50.0 mL. Place a portion of the solution in a 1.00 cm quartz cuvette and measure an absorbance of $A_1 = 0.680$ at 230 nm. At this wavelength, the molar absorptivity of K is $\varepsilon = 8.50 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{L\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot cm^{-1}}$. M ions and $Cl^-$ do not absorb at this wavelength, and at this HCl concentration almost all M is present as K.
Step 2: Transfer 10.00 mL of the solution above, add 10.00 mL of 0.100 mol·L$^{-1}$ $AgNO_3$ solution, stir thoroughly to complete precipitation, and filter. Measure the absorbance of the filtrate under the same conditions, obtaining $A_2 = 0.306$. After addition of $AgNO_3$, the amount of excess $Ag^+$ is negligible. Ignore dissolution of $AgCl$ and activity-coefficient effects.
1.3.1 Calculate the equilibrium concentration of free $Cl^-$ in the filtrate after reaction with the $AgNO_3$ solution.
